title: Companies Act, 2013 — Section 336 (Offences by officers of companies in liquidation)

content.overview: An officer (present or former) of a company that is being wound up (or is subsequently ordered or resolves to be wound up) commits an offence if, among other things, he fails to disclose fully and truly the company’s property and dispositions, fails to deliver property or books to the Company Liquidator, conceals or removes property, makes material omissions in statements, pawns or disposes of property obtained on credit and not paid for, or is guilty of false representation or fraud to obtain creditors’ consent. Punishment is imprisonment of not less than three years (up to five years) and fine of not less than one lakh (up to three lakh) rupees, with a defence of no intent to defraud or conceal. Receivers of pawned/pledged property knowing the circumstances are also punishable.
content.glance: Officers who conceal, fail to deliver, or fraudulently deal with company property or books in liquidation face mandatory minimum imprisonment and fine; receivers of tainted property are also liable.
content.study: Section 336 criminalises a range of misconduct by officers of companies in liquidation. The person must be or have been an officer of a company that, at the time of the alleged offence, is being wound up (by Tribunal or voluntarily) or is subsequently ordered or resolves to be wound up. The prohibited acts include non-disclosure of property and dispositions (except ordinary-course dispositions), failure to deliver property or books to the liquidator, concealment or removal of property, material omissions in statements relating to the company’s affairs, pawning or disposing of property obtained on credit and not paid for within a relevant period, and false representation or fraud to obtain creditors’ consent. The statutory penalty is imprisonment of not less than three years and up to five years, together with fine of not less than one lakh and up to three lakh rupees. It is a good defence if the accused proves he had no intent to defraud or to conceal the true state of affairs or to defeat the law. A person who takes in pawn or pledge or otherwise receives property knowing it was pawned, pledged or disposed of in circumstances amounting to an offence under the section is also punishable with the same range of imprisonment and a higher fine band.

sections.heading: Offences by officers
sections.body: Non-disclosure, non-delivery of property/books, concealment, material omissions, credit-property disposal, false representation/fraud — punishable with 3–5 years’ imprisonment and fine.

sections.heading: Defence and receivers
sections.body: No intent to defraud/conceal/defeat the law is a defence. Knowing receivers of tainted property are also punishable.

provisions.title: Offences by officers of companies in liquidation

examples.title: Failure to deliver books
examples.body: A former director of a company in Tribunal winding up fails to deliver the company’s books of account that are in his custody to the Company Liquidator. He commits an offence under s. 336 unless he can show absence of intent to defraud or conceal.

hypotheticals.question: Is intent to defraud an essential element of every s. 336 offence?
hypotheticals.analysis: The section provides a defence if the accused proves he had no intent to defraud or to conceal the true state of affairs or to defeat the law; the prosecution does not have to prove intent as a positive element in every case, but the defence is available.

misconceptions.trap: Only current directors can be prosecuted under s. 336.
misconceptions.correction: The section applies to any person who is or has been an officer of the company.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a Section 336 problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Confirm the person is/was an officer and the company is/was in (or subsequently enters) winding up. II. Map the conduct to a listed offence. III. Consider the no-intent defence and any receiver liability.
